subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Wisdom of Crowds
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Wisdom of Crowds.

hook.text: In 1906, a crowd guessed an ox's weight. The average was off by just one pound. No individual was that close.

buildup.text: James Surowiecki showed that diverse, independent groups often outperform individual experts.

discovery.text: Aggregation cancels individual errors. Each person's bias goes in a different direction, leaving the truth.

twist.text: It only works when judgments are independent. Let people see each other's answers and herding kills it.

climax.text: Prediction markets, Wikipedia, and jury systems all tap crowd wisdom—when structured to avoid groupthink.

punchline.text: Many independent minds beat one brilliant one.

quiz.question: What condition is required for crowd wisdom to work?
options: Judgments must be independent of each other

details.summary: Under the right conditions, the average judgment of many independent people outperforms individual experts. Key conditions include diversity of opinion, independence from each other, decentralization, and a mechanism for aggregation. When these fail, crowds become mobs.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding when crowds are wise and when they are not helps design better prediction markets, surveys, and collective decision-making systems.
takeaways: Averaged independent judgments often beat individual experts
Diversity and independence are essential for crowd wisdom
Social influence and groupthink destroy crowd accuracy

faq.question: When do crowds fail?
faq.answer: Crowds fail when members influence each other, creating herding effects. Social media amplifies this: seeing others' opinions destroys the independence that makes crowd wisdom work. Groupthink, emotional contagion, and information cascades can make crowds spectacularly wrong.

faq.question: How is crowd wisdom used in practice?
faq.answer: Prediction markets aggregate diverse opinions into probability estimates. The Delphi method collects expert judgments independently. Wikipedia aggregates diverse knowledge. Machine learning ensembles use the same principle: averaging many independent models outperforms any single model.
